question: us-policy-positions:technology-privacy.age-verification-for-social-media
definition: yes = a state law requiring social media platforms to verify users' ages (or obtain verified parental consent for minors) is in force and enforceable on 1/1/2026 (not enjoined); no = no such law, or the law is enjoined/struck or not yet effective on 1/1/2026. App-store and adult-content age laws do not count.
summarySource: Wikipedia 'Online age verification laws in the United States' (fetched 9/28/2026) as the complete tracker; Supreme Court order 25A97 (8/14/2025); Fifth Circuit No. 24-60341 (4/17/2025); Tennessee General Assembly HB1891 page; Fla. Stat. 501.1736 (flsenate.gov); Va. Code 59.1-577.1; Utah PI order (9/10/2024); SC HB 3431 page; news reports for LA, NE, TX, VA injunctions.

conflicts.readings: Yes: HB 3 bars under-14 accounts and requires parental consent for 14- and 15-year-olds, enforceable after the 11th Circuit's 11/25/2025 stay. No: the statute text sets no explicit age-verification method or 'verified' consent standard.

No: SB 162 was permanently enjoined 12/15/2025. Possible yes: HB 61 (R.S. 9:2717.1), in force since 8/1/2024, requires written parental consent before an online service contracts with a minor, though without any age-verification duty.

No: the SCOPE Act's age-verification provisions were preliminarily enjoined 2/7/2025. Possible yes: unenjoined parts still require age registration and parental-identity verification for parental tools.

No: the district court preliminarily enjoined the whole act on 9/10/2024. Ambiguity: Wikipedia says 'a week later the injunction was stayed by the district court' (likely a stay of proceedings, not of the injunction).
